title: Why does a Crown Court case take so long to reach trial?
summary: Cases wait for court time and for the people needed for a trial to be ready on the same date. In England and Wales, 25% of trials in the April to June 2026 effectiveness measure did not start as scheduled and needed another date.

process.title: From a first hearing to a Crown Court outcome

steps.label: The magistrates’ court sends the case to the Crown Court
steps.text: Criminal cases normally start in the magistrates’ court. Serious offences go to the Crown Court, and some offences can be tried in either court. Some cases go to the Crown Court for sentencing or appeal.

steps.label: Take a plea and prepare the case
steps.text: At the Crown Court the judge deals with the plea and can give directions for trial preparation. A guilty plea can take the case to sentencing. For a contested case, staff, prosecution and defence work toward a trial date.

steps.label: List the trial and make sure it can go ahead
steps.text: Listing must match a courtroom, judge, lawyers, witnesses and other requirements such as an interpreter. A trial that fails to start as scheduled and needs another date is recorded as ineffective.

steps.label: Hear the case and record the outcome
steps.text: A trial resolves the contested charges by a verdict and there may be a separate sentencing hearing. Cases can close in other ways, such as a guilty plea or prosecution discontinuance. The statistics track cases closed across these routes.

year-old-cases.title: Crown Court cases open at least a year
year-old-cases.description: The published queue of cases at least a year old grew over the three selected dates.
year-old-cases.note: England and Wales. Cases with a known age. Points are selected quarter ends from the same September 2026 release.

trial-outcomes.title: What happened at the trial listing
trial-outcomes.note: The 7,766 trials in the effectiveness breakdown form the denominator. Trials vacated in advance are reported separately. Percentages are rounded.

old-cases.title: The oldest cases are growing faster than the overall queue
old-cases.text: Open cases rose 3% in the year to June 2026. Cases open for at least a year rose 22%, from 19,384 to 23,706. The median age of an open case rose from 168 to 203 days.

consequences.text: The audit found that longer waits can add stress for victims, witnesses and defendants. More than half of cases open at least a year in June 2026 involved violence against the person or sexual offences.

old-cases.measure: Publish the age distribution of the cases still open as well as time to resolution. Follow the oldest cohorts through trial or another outcome and keep offence and remand status visible.

lost-dates.title: A trial date can pass without the trial starting
lost-dates.text: In April to June 2026, 25% of trials in the effectiveness measure were ineffective and needed another date. Of those, 27% were attributed to overlisting, 24% to the defence or prosecution not being ready, and 12% to defendant absence.

consequences.text: Relisting adds time and can require victims and witnesses to arrange attendance again. Some defendants remain on remand while they wait. Expanding court time is only one part of making a listed date usable.

lost-dates.measure: Follow the trial from the first booked date to the date it actually starts. Record reasons for relisting, repeat relistings and days on remand.

delivery-check.question: How will the Ministry of Justice show that reforms shorten waits?
delivery-check.answer: The Public Accounts Committee criticised the lack of a sufficiently ambitious plan in March 2025. Ministers later reported uncapped sitting days and published updated projections linked to the Courts and Tribunals Bill. The projections are estimates under assumptions about capacity, reform and efficiency.
delivery-check.watch: Ask for a comparison with published outcomes, including open cases a year or more old and repeated relistings. Check separately which reforms have come into force.

takeaways.label: Cases still open
takeaways.text: The Crown Court had 80,829 open cases in June 2026. Of the cases with recorded age, 23,706 had been open a year or more.

takeaways.label: The trial date
takeaways.text: 25% of trials in the trial-effectiveness measure for April to June 2026 did not start as scheduled and needed a new date.

takeaways.label: What progress looks like
takeaways.text: Look for fewer long-waiting cases and fewer rescheduled trials, alongside the numbers coming into and leaving the court.

outcomes.heading: Why completed cases tell a different story
outcomes.text: For defendants dealt with at the Crown Court in April to June 2026, the median time from case receipt to the first main hearing was 11.3 weeks. For those dealt with by jury trial following a not guilty plea it was 49.7 weeks. The measure is calculated when the case closes. The age of open cases shows how long those cases have waited so far.

outcomes.heading: Test capacity by what happens to real cases
outcomes.text: Extra court days can help, but courtrooms, staff and lawyers have to be available at the same time. A lasting improvement would show up in completed cases, fewer ineffective trials and less time waiting for people in the longest-running cases.

cost-and-funding.heading: Funding to sit and funding to finish cases
cost-and-funding.text: The National Audit Office records 111,250 funded Crown Court sitting days in 2025/26, compared with 81,899 in 2019/20. The government says it has removed the cap on sitting days. The Ministry of Justice separately reported £287 million committed in 2026/27 for court estate repairs and digital upgrades across jurisdictions. Court staff, judges, legal aid, prosecution and remand create costs across different budgets.

cost-and-funding.heading: What a cost per completed case should include
cost-and-funding.text: Follow the costs of preparing the case and each listing through resolution, including time and custody costs when the trial is relisted. The sources here do not give a joined-up cost of a typical delayed case.

whats-changing.heading: Use the reform baselines when the next figures arrive
whats-changing.text: The government’s October response to the Leveson review sets out proposals to keep more cases in the magistrates’ courts and to permit judge-alone trials for certain technical and lengthy fraud and financial cases. Its projections depend on court capacity and estimated efficiencies. Check the age of the queue and trial effectiveness in both courts against those assumptions.
